flashcards.q: In this round, who picks which resume bullets get drilled, and why does that matter for preparation?
flashcards.a: The interviewer picks, not the candidate. This means every bullet needs to be prepared to real depth, not just the 3 favorite rehearsed stories -- the test is specifically whether depth is uniform across the resume or concentrated in a few spots.

flashcards.q: What resume error must be corrected unprompted the moment the vLLM/SageMaker bullet comes up, and what are the real values?
flashcards.a: 'ml.4xlarge' and 'g4.2xlarge' are not real SageMaker instance identifiers. Real ones are almost certainly ml.g4dn.2xlarge and ml.g5.xlarge. Correcting it cleanly and without defensiveness is the actual signal; the error itself is forgivable.

flashcards.q: For the 8-service platform bullet, what's the strong answer to 'if you had to cut two people and had half the timeline, which of these eight would not exist?'
flashcards.a: A real prioritization with a stated reason -- event and context path first, because a recommender with no context is a popularity list. Not 'we needed all eight,' which reveals no ordering logic behind the scope.

flashcards.q: For the 89% ETL latency reduction bullet, what's the first follow-up a technically literate hiring manager asks, and why is it the weakest part of the story as written?
flashcards.a: 'What was actually consuming the 4.5 hours?' The story as documented gives the before/after numbers but not the root bottleneck (sequential stages, unpartitioned reads, a skewed join, single-node processing) -- repeating the headline number without this is the single most attackable gap on this bullet.

flashcards.q: Why is 'nine times faster' on the ETL story an incomplete answer, and what follow-up exposes it?
flashcards.a: 'Nine times faster sometimes just means nine times more compute spend.' A candidate who hasn't considered the cost side of their own signature performance metric reads as someone who optimized one dimension without checking the other.

flashcards.q: For the OWASP/cross-tenant authorization bullet, what's the strong answer to 'how loudly did you escalate it, and to whom?'
flashcards.a: A concrete reproduction written up (not a vague concern), escalated immediately rather than quietly patched (a silent fix leaves nobody able to assess exposure), fixed at the object-fetch layer as a class fix rather than patching only discovered instances.

flashcards.q: For the ClickHouse OOM bullet, what's the honest answer to 'gc.collect() is a workaround, not the real fix -- why didn't you build it right the first time?'
flashcards.a: Admit it plainly: streaming with generators and bounded batches so no large object graph ever exists is the structural fix; gc.collect() compensates for allocator behavior rather than eliminating memory pressure. Admitting the first fix was expedient is stronger than defending it as ideal.

flashcards.q: For the MongoDB race-conditions bullet, what does 'your test suite passed the whole time this bug existed' actually reveal, and what should change?
flashcards.a: Both bug classes (race conditions, event-loop errors) are invisible at parallelism one, which is the concurrency level most test suites run at by default. The real fix isn't complete without a CI concurrency test that runs the hot path above production peak parallelism.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between the answer 'I built all eight services' and a strong answer to 'which parts specifically did you write'?
flashcards.a: A strong answer differentiates: which services had direct personal code contribution vs. architecture/design ownership with review vs. delegation -- precision about scope of authorship, not a blanket claim of having built everything personally.

flashcards.q: What's the hardest version of the scope-calibration question, and why is it deliberately the hardest?
flashcards.a: 'Name one thing outside your own code that other engineers had to change because of a decision you made.' It's deliberately hard because this is a genuinely thin area on this resume -- the strong answer is an honest one even if it's 'I have one strong example and not a second as strong,' not a manufactured second claim.

flashcards.q: What's the real test behind 'why are you leaving,' and what follow-up checks for coherence?
flashcards.a: Whether the stated reason is forward-looking, specific, and not disparaging the current employer. Coherence check: 'if your current company offered you this exact role and scope, would you stay?' -- an answer revealing pure compensation motivation with nothing structural is legitimate but weaker than one naming something the current employer structurally cannot offer.

flashcards.q: For the manager-disagreement question, what does the follow-up 'would you have escalated further if your manager's manager overruled you?' actually test?
flashcards.a: Whether the disagreement was really about being right or about a safe, low-stakes battle. Strong answer: a stated threshold for when to let a technical disagreement go (low-stakes) vs. escalate further (real correctness/safety consequences) -- not claiming to fight every battle regardless of stakes.

flashcards.q: Why is the order of this round's rounds within a full loop deliberate (coding -> design -> AI depth -> behavioral -> HM grill)?
flashcards.a: HM grill runs last because it's closest to how most real onsites close -- with the person who has to defend the hire internally -- and because it tests whether depth and honesty persist after four rounds of cumulative fatigue, not just at the start of the day.

flashcards.q: What must be true about the STAR bank's [CONFIRM: ...] markers before this round can be run for a real score?
flashcards.a: They must be resolved with real numbers first -- team size, adoption counts, measurement methods. Running the round with placeholder gaps still in the source material means the round can't score correctness/depth meaningfully, since the ground truth itself is incomplete.

flashcards.q: What's the STRONG NO HIRE tell in this round, distinct from just getting facts wrong?
flashcards.a: Not noticing, or getting defensive about, a direct factual correction from the interviewer (e.g. the SageMaker instance names) -- the inability to cleanly absorb a correction is a bigger red flag than the original error.
